item.title: MiBeeNvr: A Lightweight Home NVR System I Built
item.description:
I have several cameras at home — a few Xiaomi cameras, some DIY ESP32 cameras, and multiple Raspberry Pi CSI cameras. I’d been using cloud storage solutions, but I was never comfortable with them: vendor lock-in, network dependency, and the costs add up. So I decided to build my own NVR system, called MiBeeNvr.

Why Build MiBeeNvr

To be honest, I was never satisfied with existing cloud storage solutions. Take Xiaomi cameras, for example. By default, you can only view them through the Mi Home app. Recordings are either stored on an SD card (limited capacity, frequent plugging/unplugging) or in the cloud. Cloud storage costs tens of dollars per month, and there’s the privacy concern — you never know when the manufacturer might use your video data for AI training or sell it to third parties. Not to mention vendor lock-in — switching platforms is nearly impossible.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.2.0: Live View and Auto-Merging
item.description:
v0.1.0 could only play back recordings — no live view; it shipped binaries only, so Docker users had to roll their own image; recordings landed as 30-second segments, 2,880 files per camera per day; and every camera shared one retention setting, so the front door and the balcony couldn’t be treated differently. v0.2.0 fixes all of that in one go.

Live view, finally

  • Click in the web UI and the live picture plays — nothing to install, H.264 and H.265 both supported
  • Switches to the low-resolution stream automatically when bandwidth is tight
  • Consumes nothing while nobody is watching

Easier to install

  • Two Docker commands and it runs — Raspberry-Pi-class ARM devices included
  • No config file needed on first start; setup happens in the web UI
  • Docker-less Linux machines install with one command and register as a boot-time system service
  • Works on phones too; Chinese/English switchable; light/dark follows the system

Recordings that behave

  • Fragments merge automatically — small segments become large files, faster to manage and search
  • Per-camera retention: keep the front door 30 days, the balcony 7
  • Storage trends and per-camera recording volume visible in the web UI
  • Cheap ESP32-CAM-class cameras connect directly — no protocol conversion to wrestle with

The previous article introduced MiBeeNvr’s basic features and design philosophy. It’s only been a week since v0.1.0, and v0.2.0 follows right behind. This update is substantial — 15 new features, some I needed myself, others from community feedback.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.3.0: One-Click Xiaomi Camera Integration, Recordings Never Lost
item.description:
Got Xiaomi cameras at home? Want to keep your recordings on your own storage instead of relying on the cloud?

As someone with several Xiaomi cameras at home, I always had one frustration: every time I wanted to check the footage from my doorbell camera, I had to log into Xiaomi Cloud, wait for ages while it loaded, and it would often just spin. Plus, cloud storage charges by the day — it adds up over the month. And if you swap cameras, all your old recordings are gone. Pretty frustrating.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.3.1: Multi-Protocol Streaming and Native Xiaomi Camera Support
item.description:
#XQ|A lot of work went into the releases after v0.2.0. v0.3.x brings several major updates: native Xiaomi camera support, recording archiving, multi-protocol streaming architecture (WebRTC/HTTP-FLV/RTMP/SRT/LL-HLS), and a wave of security hardening. The architectural evolution from external dependencies to built-in implementation, from single protocol to full protocol support, was much more complex than I expected.

The previous post introduced v0.2.0’s 15 new features (v0.2.0 Update). If you haven’t read the first post, start with MiBeeNvr Introduction. v0.3.0 focuses on deep Xiaomi camera integration, and v0.3.1 builds on that with a complete multi-protocol streaming architecture. For the full changelog, see GitHub Release Notes.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.4.0: Audio Recording Pipeline and Multi-Layer Health Monitoring Architecture
item.description:
After v0.3.1 shipped, v0.4.0 is a feature-dense release: audio recording pipeline, multi-layer health monitoring engine, HLS/LL-HLS playback stability optimization, and a major UI redesign. For the full changelog, see GitHub Release Notes.

The previous post covered v0.3.x’s multi-protocol streaming and Xiaomi camera support (MiBeeNvr v0.3.1 Tech Post). If you haven’t read the first post, start with MiBeeNvr Introduction.

Audio Recording: From Silent to Sound

In the v0.3.x era, recorded MP4 files only had a video track. v0.4.0 introduces a complete audio capture and muxing pipeline, supporting AAC audio from RTSP cameras and G.711 audio from ONVIF/Xiaomi cameras.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.5.0: Full ONVIF and Hardware Transcoding
item.description:
ONVIF cameras could be discovered and their stream URL retrieved — but that was just a corner of ONVIF: PTZ control, picture adjustment, and event subscription, the parts you actually use daily, were missing. And plenty of cameras output H.265 only, which browsers can’t play directly.

PTZ and picture, adjustable

  • Drive the camera with a joystick in the web UI — pan, zoom, one-tap home
  • Presets can be created, invoked, and deleted; frequent viewpoints are one tap away
  • Brightness, contrast, saturation, and sharpness adjust live on sliders, effective immediately
  • Events the camera reports (motion detection, alarms) show up in the web UI in real time

H.265 cameras play in the browser

  • Encoding is detected automatically; H.265 is transcoded to browser-playable H.264 on hardware when needed
  • Freeze-frame anti-flicker keeps the picture smooth through the transition
  • A new transcoding monitor page shows task status and performance at a glance

Steadier

  • The Xiaomi-camera disconnect churn is fixed: a full buffer drops the oldest frame instead of tearing down the whole session
  • Reconnects moved to tiered backoff with jitter — several cameras dropping at once no longer avalanche
  • A batch of fixes: first-boot Docker crash, false health alarms, a login-redirect loop

A protocol isn’t supported until all of it is.

item.title: MiBeeNvr's AI Detection: Why Inference Runs in the Browser, and Why YOLO11n
item.description:
MiBeeNvr’s Smart Features include an AI detection option that runs inference entirely in the browser — the backend server does no inference at all. The ONNX model file is served to the browser, and ONNX Runtime Web executes it client-side. The model is Ultralytics’ yolo11n.onnx.

This isn’t a common choice among NVR products. Most open-source NVRs (Frigate, the go2rtc ecosystem) put AI inference on the backend, because the backend has access to the raw stream, runs persistently, and can use a GPU. Moving inference into the browser is a deliberate architectural trade-off, not a stopgap. This post breaks down two things: why inference lives in the browser, and — given that premise — why YOLO11n.

item.title: Comprehensive Survey: NVR P2P Remote Access Technologies
item.description:
How do NVR (Network Video Recorder) systems let mobile apps view surveillance feeds from any network? This is a core requirement for the security industry and smart home ecosystems. This article systematically surveys three dimensions: open-source NVR projects (Frigate, go2rtc, Kerberos.io, Agent DVR, etc.), commercial surveillance vendors (Hikvision, Dahua, EZVIZ, Ubiquiti, Synology, Reolink, etc.), and third-party P2P platforms and security research (TUTK Kalay, iLnkP2P/PPPP, GB/T 28181, key CVEs).

All technical descriptions are verified against primary sources—official documentation, security advisories, and academic papers. Key statistics include citations.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.6.0: Timelapse and Transcoding
item.description:
Once recording is up and running, the disk cries first: one 1080p camera writes tens of GB a day, and 30-day retention eats most of a 1TB drive. The community reported the same thing over and over, and timelapse plus transcoding came up as the favored fixes.

Less disk

  • Timelapse: cameras whose scenes sit still most of the day need roughly 5% of the space for the same duration
  • Frames are skipped automatically while the picture stays static — idle time isn’t wasted
  • The extraction interval is configurable, and multiple cameras stagger themselves instead of spiking together

Recordings can be transcoded

  • H.264 ↔ H.265 in both directions, with historical recordings backfillable
  • Hardware encoding is auto-detected: use it when present (the Banana Pi M5 saturates H.265 hardware encoding), disable cleanly when not — the Raspberry Pi 3B is unaffected
  • Transcoding starts from the web UI, with status and progress visible

Steadier playback, easier diagnosis

  • A frozen picture is detected automatically
  • A class of H.265 playback corruption is fixed
  • Prometheus metrics and remote logging are wired in — problems get diagnosed from data instead of guesses

Keep the disk alive first.

item.title: H.264 / H.265 / H.266 Web Frontend Playback: Which Generation to Pick in 2026
item.description: In the MiBee NVR surveillance-dashboard project, should the frontend pull H.264 or H.265 from all 16 cameras? A seemingly simple question that gets deeper the more you dig. H.265 needs only half the bitrate of H.264 at the same quality, saving both bandwidth and storage. But plenty of online sources still claim “H.265 browser support is poor, Firefox doesn’t support it, you need to install extensions.” Which of these claims still hold?

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.6.0's Test Machines: Three Camera Projects Updated in Sync
item.description: The concurrently released MiBeeNvr v0.6.0 brought major features like timelapse, video transcoding, and ONVIF enhancements. Unit tests alone are far from enough — the full workflow must be tested against real camera hardware. To provide reliable test machines for this release, three camera projects were updated on the same day, June 5th — both to supply testing environments for the NVR and to solve some typical embedded development engineering problems along the way.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.7.0: Timelapse v2 and the Hard-Fix Release
item.description:
After v0.6.0 shipped the timelapse pipeline, community feedback quickly listed the hard problems: an intermediate JPEG sequence ate too much space; H.265 cameras produced unplayable timelapse segments; dual-lens Xiaomi devices could only grab the main lens; and H.265 live view occasionally crashed outright.

Timelapse that actually works

  • Merging no longer goes through intermediate images: much smaller footprint, and the merged output is directly playable video
  • Timelapse segments from H.265 cameras play properly now
  • Merge windows come in selectable tiers (8 hours to 30 days) instead of a fixed daily run
  • Timelapse and regular recordings share one list — no flipping between two pages

Dual-lens Xiaomi, lens selectable

  • Dual-lens devices like the CW500 and Outdoor Cam 4 can target a specific lens
  • Chosen in the web UI, effective immediately

Steadier

  • The H.265 live-view crash is thoroughly fixed
  • The transcoding module was refactored into layers — adding new encoders or hardware no longer ripples through the whole pipeline

Fix what hurts first.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.9.0: Zero-Config Discovery, Debts Repaid
item.description:
As the camera count grows, so do the annoyances: adding an ONVIF camera meant typing IPs and opening a terminal; with 9 cameras starting together, the UI stalled for a dozen-plus seconds; every deployment began with checking whether FFmpeg was installed; and the older Xiaomi devices (Dafang, Xiaofang, Aqara G2) simply couldn’t be integrated.

Cameras that show up on their own

  • ONVIF cameras are discovered by the NVR the moment they power on; enter the password once in the web UI to activate — no IP fiddling
  • New and old devices live in one list
  • The TUTK-protocol legacy Xiaomi devices connect now too

It keeps up with many cameras

  • 9 cameras starting together no longer stall the UI (measured: 14.9 seconds down to milliseconds)
  • The storage layer was rewritten — recording writes no longer lock out queries
  • FFmpeg went from required to optional: it runs fine without it

A more complete interface

  • Missing translations and hardcoded Chinese strings fixed in one sweep
  • Recording-fragment cleanup, the Docker port clash, broken merge settings, and a batch of similar fixes

Debts get paid eventually.

item.title: ONVIF vs GB/T 28181: How They Work Inside — Plug-and-Play Devices vs System-Level Networking
item.description: After MiBeeNvr v0.9 shipped ONVIF auto-discovery, manual camera configuration was mostly gone. The next question was whether to add GB/T 28181 uplink support, so I dug through the mechanics of both protocols. Most comparison articles online stop at “ONVIF is the international standard, GB28181 is the Chinese national standard”—which carries zero information for someone writing code. This post breaks both protocols down to the signaling-flow and message level: how ONVIF discovers devices and obtains stream URIs; how GB28181’s 20-digit codes address everything, how INVITE negotiates a stream, and what PS encapsulation actually is.

item.title: The Surveillance Protocol Panorama: A Four-Layer Map from Access to Compliance — What Each Protocol Is and When to Use It
item.description: The previous post took ONVIF and GB/T 28181 apart down to signaling and messages. But building an NVR means the protocol environment extends well beyond those two: vendor-private APIs on the camera side, a view-library standard on the public-security side, Ministry-of-Transport standards for vehicles, WebRTC for browser viewing, HLS for public distribution, and a national-crypto compliance stack. This post lays out the entire landscape—each protocol gets four sections: what it is → key technical points → its relationship with other protocols → its value to an NVR. Beginners can read it as an index; veterans can jump straight to the priority table.

item.title: Dual-Stack Cameras in the Field: What Happens When ONVIF and GB28181 Run Together, and Whether GB28181 Travels
item.description:
The first two posts covered protocol mechanics and the landscape; this one returns to device-side questions an NVR builder actually meets: can a camera hang both protocol stacks at once? With both enabled, what does it cost the camera, and what does it mean for an NVR that discovers cameras via ONVIF? Finally, a product question—does GB28181 actually get used overseas, and is it worth building for international markets?

Three concepts used throughout:

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.10.0: H.265 Live View and the Big Cleanup
item.description:
H.265 cameras used to be a half-broken experience: no live view on plain-HTTP LANs (HTTPS or nothing), merged recordings frequently black-screening on Edge, and timelapse merging not working at all.

H.265 plays everywhere now

  • H.265 live view works on plain-HTTP LANs — HTTPS no longer required
  • HTTPS environments use hardware acceleration automatically; everything else falls back to software decoding — both roads lead to playback
  • Recording merges, playback, and timelapse H.265 issues fixed in one pass

Better timelapse

  • Rewritten to v3: the 1-hour merge-window cap is gone
  • Merges are recorded in the database, progress queryable

A cleaner foundation

  • Login moved to signed tokens — no server-side session dependency, expiry under control
  • An architecture cleanup across config, DI root, and API routing, paving the way for stronger AI and more cameras

Clean the foundation before building higher.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.11.0: fnOS Installs, GB/T 28181, and the Full-Day Timeline
item.description:
A few days after v0.10.0 went stable, fnOS users’ feedback boiled down to one sentence: it won’t install. Two older debts got settled in the same release: Hikvision/Dahua cameras couldn’t enroll — you either bought their NVR or stood up a separate GB platform; and playback showed one 30-second segment at a time, so reviewing a whole day meant clicking through segment by segment.

It installs now

  • All three install blockers are fixed: stalling on image downloads, a dead desktop icon, and a port field that rejected 9090 outright
  • The offline package bundles the full image set — works the moment it’s installed, no network needed
  • The online package is a few dozen KB and picks whichever of the China mirror or the official registry answers faster
  • The one-click install script auto-selects the same way
  • Synology, QNAP, and ZSpace store templates landed too

Easier to integrate

  • Hikvision/Dahua cameras enroll with a few filled-in fields — no vendor NVR, no separate platform (via the GB/T 28181 national standard)
  • Fully automatic after registration: a camera card per channel, recording starts on its own
  • PTZ, zoom, presets, and voice intercom work; the recordings on the camera’s own SD card are searchable and replayable
  • Hand Home Assistant-style integrations a dedicated key you can revoke on its own, without touching the global password
  • An IP change no longer breaks clients — they track the device, not the address

Playback that works

  • A whole day’s recordings stitch into one timeline — scrub to any moment
  • Segment switches no longer black-flash; the handover is invisible
  • Blank stretches from power cuts scrub right through without stalling
  • Authenticated live streams play on iPhone again

If it doesn’t install, it isn’t released.

item.title: The Rust and Go Ecosystems for ONVIF/GB28181: Library Selection, Source Reading, and a Hardware-Free Integration Path
item.description: The first three posts settled the protocol mechanics, the landscape, and the device side; the final question is concrete: which libraries to write it with. This survey went through everything usable in both ecosystems. The one-sentence verdict: ONVIF has workable libraries on both sides; the mature GB28181 implementations live on the Go/Java/C++ side while Rust’s are still young; and for streaming infrastructure (repackaging, distribution, egress) the Go ecosystem is clearly thicker.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.12.0: Sub-streams, Adaptive Recording, and Full-path Observability
item.description:
MiBeeNvr v0.12.0 is out. This release goes after two everyday annoyances: watching the cameras on a phone, where a thumbnail-sized preview quietly pulls the full-resolution video underneath — eating data and heating the phone; and corridor or doorway cameras writing tens of GB a day that nobody ever replays.

Less disk

  • When nothing moves, the camera records less; the moment anything moves, it snaps back to full recording without dropping a frame. Quiet scenes measured at roughly 3/4 less disk
  • A louder sound, a doorbell, or a sensor signal also kicks it back to full recording
  • The replay timeline carries a green-to-red heat strip — the segments where something happened are visible at a glance
  • When the disk nears full, the quietest recordings are deleted first
  • Phone viewing defaults to a small, smooth stream: no stutter, no heat; one tap switches to HD for detail
  • When nobody is watching, that preview stream disconnects by itself — no camera connection or bandwidth tied up
